Ten years after the original
["Why We Created Julia"](https://julialang.org/blog/2012/02/why-we-created-julia/) post,
the Julia blog asked its community to write back. About a hundred people did, each with a
short, signed note. Most of them start the same way: someone tired of prototyping in Python
or MATLAB and then rewriting the slow parts in C, who tried Julia out of curiosity and never
left. There is an R job that went from eighteen hours to five minutes, and code running on
aircraft collision-avoidance systems and lunar missions.

What I liked most is how often the story turns on a first pull request. Someone fixes a small
thing, gets a careful review or a thumbs-up from a core developer, and a few years later is
the one reviewing. That matched my own start in the Julia world, through JuliaSmoothOptimizers,
TagBot and Qiskit.jl, closely enough that reading it felt a little like reading about people
I already knew.

[Why We Use Julia, 10 Years Later](https://julialang.org/blog/2022/02/10years/), The Julia
Blog.
